# The Cup Day coolroom situation, for Jonno

Dear Jonno,

Since you’ve messaged me approximately 400 times asking what happened with the coolroom on Cup Day, here you go. I’m putting it on the blog so all 40 readers can enjoy it too. Hi Mum.

First of all, you would’ve cried.

I know you reckon you wouldn’t have, but London has made you soft. You’ve been over there since February posting photos of pints and calling everyone “mate” like you invented it. You would’ve taken one look at our coolroom that morning and booked yourself straight back to Heathrow.

I got in at 6.40 on Tuesday, Cup Day, and the coolroom thermometer was sitting at 11 degrees. Eleven. The compressor had died sometime overnight, and everything in there had been having a lovely warm evening without us.

We had 140 covers booked for lunch. Three-course set menu. Raff was away, so I was running the kitchen.

I stood there for a bit hoping the thermometer was wrong. It wasn’t.

Wally from Coldline couldn’t get to us until Wednesday, and the part had to come from Sydney anyway. So that was that. No bloke appearing with a toolbox to save the day. Just me, a warm coolroom and a booking sheet full of people who were going to expect lunch.

Phil’s contribution was “just make it work, mate.”

Cheers Phil. Hadn’t thought of that. I was planning to lie down on the floor until everybody went home, but now you’ve said that, we’ll simply make it work.

We started sorting through everything and moving what we could save. The two undercounters got filled, then the bar fridge. Marta next door let us use half her walk-in, which was an absolute lifesaver, although she has since made it very clear this was not a charitable act.

All up we lost about $1,800 of stock, mostly dairy and the duck legs. Not ideal when you’ve got a set menu and a dining room about to fill up, but there wasn’t much point standing around looking at it.

This is how Benny and I ended up taking 30 kilos of beef shin down the laneway in the rain on a milk crate trolley.

You know the trolley. The one that already looked like it had been hit by a tram.

One of the wheels fell off.

So there’s me and Benny in the rain, trying to get a trolley full of beef moving again, while people are getting ready for a nice Cup Day lunch inside. You would’ve been beside yourself. Actually, no, you would’ve stood under the awning filming it and sending it to the group chat before eventually helping.

A lady on table nine saw us out the window and later asked if the beef was “free range from the laneway”. Fair question. It had certainly seen more of Melbourne that morning than most tourists.

Meanwhile Kev had taken the old esky to the servo and filled it with ice. Fourteen bags. The bloke at the servo asked if we were having a party.

Yeah mate, massive party. Everyone’s invited. Dress code is wet apron and barely contained panic.

Kev just got on with it, like he always does. I don’t know where we’d be without him, but on Tuesday I reckon the answer would’ve been sitting in a puddle beside a warm esky.

By the time service was getting close, the place was spread across about four different fridges and Marta’s walk-in. Every time someone needed something, there was a brief discussion about which suburb we’d put it in. We made it to lunch, though, and somehow the food started going out.

At 12.15 we had to 86 the panna cotta.

You know that feeling when you’ve been holding it together all morning and then one more thing goes wrong and you just have to laugh? That was the panna cotta. Sorry to everyone who was looking forward to it, but there was no panna cotta coming.

Dessert became “affogato with whatever”.

And people loved it. More than they probably would’ve liked the panna cotta we’d actually planned. I don’t know what to do with that information. Maybe next Cup Day we’ll put “whatever” on the set menu from the start and save ourselves a lot of trouble.

Honestly, though, it was the best service we’ve done all year. Everyone was locked in. Benny was flying, Kev kept us going, and somehow all 140 people got fed despite half the kitchen living next door. Even Phil’s plan worked, if you’re willing to call it a plan.

Marta has decided we’re paying her back in croissant credit. I owe her about three weeks of staff meal at this point. I don’t know how the exchange rate works, and I’m pretty sure she’s making it up as she goes, but after letting us take over half her walk-in she can have what she wants.

Oh, and my horse in the sweep was called **Ice Cold Lad**. Came second last.

Of course it did. The universe was having a great day.

Anyway, that’s the story. Bistro kitchens run on bar fridges and spite, and apparently so do I.

You missed a good one, mate. You would’ve hated every second of it, then spent the next ten years telling people how you saved Cup Day single-handedly.

Come home, ya flog.
